activities.anchor: Plant two trees of the same species
activities.caption: bet before you read on
activities.name: laTwoTreesPredict

config.q: Same species, same planting day — ten years on, what does the designer expect to find?
choices: Two near-identical trees — same species, same day
Two different plants — one thriving, one struggling
config.why: No two sites are identical — and that simple observation separates landscape architecture from its neighbouring disciplines: the medium is alive, and it bends the whole process.

activities.caption: file each finding under the system it belongs to
activities.name: laInventoryBuckets

config.prompt: A first walk around the site — file each finding under its system:
buckets: life on and around the site

items.label: the sun's path across the seasons, and frost pockets
where rain arrives, flows, pools and exits
profiles, drainage, compaction, bearing capacity, pH
existing trees worth keeping, root zones protected
what deserves framing, what deserves screening
how people actually move — often not how the plan assumes
the site's history and the neighbourhood's habits

config.why: None of it is decoration for a report — every item is a constraint or an opportunity with a construction consequence.

activities.caption: rebuild the suitability method in sequence
activities.name: laSuitabilityOrder

config.prompt: Suitability analysis runs in a fixed sequence — rebuild it:
items: Survey the site and collect the facts
Map each factor on its own sheet — slope, soil, drainage, habitat
Overlay the sheets (translucent film then, GIS layers today)
Read the overlays for where building, planting and play belong
Let the analysis generate the design — the nuisance re-cast as a feature
config.why: What distinguishes professional analysis from decoration is that it generates the design rather than merely preceding it.

activities.anchor: The studio's method is a process and a pedagogy
activities.caption: pair each studio term with its work
activities.name: laStudioMatch

config.prompt: From bubble diagram to built work — pair the term with its job:

pairs.right: states what the design must achieve: uses, areas, adjacencies, budget
spaces as bubbles, relationships as arrows — kitchen near terrace, play visible from kitchen, service hidden
one diagram that explains the whole composition — 'a spine path threading three garden rooms'
the budget cuts that will certainly come — a strong parti survives them, a weak one dissolves into decoration

config.why: The reason for bubbles is economic: it is far cheaper to move a circle than a wall.

activities.anchor: speaks in contour lines and spot elevations
activities.caption: buy gradient with distance — Fermi-style
activities.name: laGradingEstimate

config.prompt: A walkway must climb 0.45 m. At the 5 per cent comfortable maximum for an accessible path, how long a run does the climb need?
config.why: 0.45 ÷ 0.05 = 9 m. Over the 15 m this site offers, 5 per cent would demand 0.75 m of fall — more than the 0.45 m available: hence switchbacks, terraces or regrading.
config.context: The calculation is elementary; the judgement — where to spend fall, where to buy it back — is landscape architecture.

activities.anchor: spacing that looks gappy on day one
activities.caption: stack the planting layers top to bottom
activities.name: laLayerOrder

config.prompt: The palette composes in functional layers — stack them from the canopy down:
config.why: Every plant is placed by mature size: you are drawing the garden of year ten, not the one at installation.

activities.anchor: a flat site is a good site
activities.caption: find the line the grading logic refutes
activities.name: laGradingSpot

config.prompt: One line of this grading summary is wrong — click it:
lines: A gently regraded landscape — 1–2 per cent away from buildings, toward an inlet or a rain garden — drains itself quietly for free.
Level ground is the easiest ground to drain.
A truly flat plaza either ponds or needs engineered drainage everywhere.
Grading is design done in metres of rise and fall, not cleanup performed afterwards.
config.correction: Level ground is the hardest ground to drain.
config.why: The misconception inverts the logic: water needs slope, so level ground is the problem to solve — and grading is design done in metres of rise and fall.

activities.anchor: from stormwater parks to landscape urbanism
activities.caption: scrub the canon — six traditions in date order
activities.name: laCanonTimeline

events.title: The formal tradition
events.text: Persian paradise gardens and Italian Renaissance terraces reach their apotheosis in André Le Nôtre's Versailles (from the 1660s): axes, parterres, fountains, clipped hedging — the landscape as order and dominion.

events.title: The English landscape garden
events.text: The eighteenth century (William Kent, Capability Brown, Humphry Repton) rejects the geometric for the apparently natural: rolling lawns, serpentine lakes, and the ha-ha — the sunken wall that keeps livestock out without a visible fence.

events.title: The public park
events.text: Olmsted and Vaux's Greensward plan wins the Central Park competition: scenery in cities argued as a public-health instrument — the founding act of landscape architecture as a modern profession.

events.title: The modern movement
events.text: Mid-twentieth century (Thomas Church, Garrett Eckbo, Dan Kiley): ornament stripped, gardens composed as outdoor rooms for modern living.

events.title: The ecological turn
events.text: McHarg's Design with Nature turns the brief from scenery to system: read the natural processes, design with them, measure success in function as well as beauty.
